Learning from Hindsight for VLA Reinforcement Learning

Iris Xu1, Sunshine Jiang1, John Marangola1, Pulkit Agrawal1, Zhang-Wei Hong2 1Massachusetts Institute of Technology  2MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab
Abstract

Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to fine-tune vision-language-action (VLA) models, but robot interaction is expensive and learning becomes highly sample inefficient when successful rollouts are rare. When reward is assigned only for completing the commanded task, a failed rollout is treated as having no value even if it successfully executes behaviors relevant to that task. A robot that fails to place the correct object in a bowl may still move that object toward the bowl or place a different object inside it, demonstrating objects and actions that can be reused to solve the target task. These behaviors define auxiliary tasks that the policy can already solve, providing useful learning signals even before it can solve the harder target task. We introduce Learning from Hindsight (LfH), which turns such failures into additional learning signals. Using a pretrained vision-language model, LfH relabels failed rollouts with the behaviors they actually accomplish and trains the policy jointly on the commanded task and these auxiliary tasks. On out-of-distribution LIBERO-PRO manipulation tasks, LfH matches the final performance of GRPO with approximately 5×5\times fewer rollouts and improves sample efficiency across multiple VLA backbones. On a physical Franka robot, LfH raises success from 0%0\% to 56%56\% within 160 training rollouts, while GRPO reaches 22%22\%.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) [8] is increasingly used to fine-tune vision-language-action (VLA) models for robot control [3, 5]. A typical pipeline adapts a VLA to a new task by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a few teleoperated demonstrations, then continues with RL so that the robot improves from its own interaction. But when the initial policy rarely succeeds, most rollouts receive no reward and contribute little to learning, making RL fine-tuning highly sample inefficient.

A failed rollout, however, is not necessarily useless data. In Figure 1, every attempt at “Put the green container in the bowl” fails, yet one rollout puts the tape in the bowl and another moves the green container toward it. Each rollout succeeds at some task, so relabeling it with the instruction it did satisfy turns a failure into a success. These hindsight tasks are also building blocks of the target task: one placing an object in the bowl and the other moving the green container. Because VLAs generalize compositionally over familiar objects and skills [4, 33], learning these building blocks helps the policy put them together.

This strategy, known as hindsight relabeling, is well established in goal-conditioned RL. Hindsight experience replay [1] relabels a trajectory that misses its goal with the outcome it actually reached, and later work extends the idea to richer goal spaces such as images [18, 17, 6, 19]. In these settings, relabeling is straightforward, because the outcome a trajectory reached is directly observable and can serve as its goal. For a language-conditioned VLA, however, the instruction a rollout satisfied is not observed and must be inferred from the robot’s behavior. Prior language relabeling for robots operates offline, deriving new instructions for fixed datasets from existing annotations or primitive behaviors [28, 7, 23]. Inferring what a failed rollout accomplished while the policy is still being trained remains an open problem.

Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) [24] offer a natural way to infer what a robot accomplished. Given a rollout video, a VLM can describe the robot’s behavior in open-ended language, and this description can replace the rollout’s original instruction. Using these labels for RL fine-tuning, however, raises two challenges. First, a VLM asked to describe a rollout will usually produce some instruction, even when the robot only moved accidentally, and its labels can be poorly grounded in the scene. Second, relabeled rollouts are off-policy, because the policy produced them while following a different instruction, so the update must correct for this mismatch.

We propose Learning from Hindsight (LfH), which relabels failed rollouts with a VLM during RL fine-tuning and addresses both challenges. For the first, LfH treats relabeling as a constrained judgment rather than free-form captioning. The VLM is grounded in the objects present in the scene and may answer that a rollout accomplished nothing. A separate query then checks whether rollouts actually complete the hindsight instruction and may answer unsure when the outcome is ambiguous, so a label that does not match the behavior earns little or no reward. In our ablation on LIBERO-PRO Goal, removing any of these options reduces the gains of LfH (Section A.1). For the second, the exact correction [18] multiplies probability ratios across every step of the trajectory, a product that vanishes or explodes over long VLA horizons. LfH instead corrects only for the state and action at each step, accepting a small bias in exchange for much lower variance (Section A.2).

Our principal contribution is showing that VLMs can turn failed rollouts into useful training data for VLAs. On LIBERO-PRO [31] manipulation tasks whose instructions differ from those seen in demonstrations, LfH matches the final performance of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [21] with approximately 5×5\times fewer rollouts. It also outperforms learned progress rewards [13, 11], which measure progress only on the commanded task. These gains hold across VLA backbones and extend to a real Franka robot, where, within 160 training rollouts, LfH raises success from 0%0\% to 56%56\% while GRPO reaches 22%22\%.

2 Related Work

Hindsight and Language Relabeling. Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) [1] relabels a trajectory with the goal it actually achieved, and later work extends the idea to image goals [19]. Language relabeling has mostly been used to enlarge offline datasets. Zhang et al. [30] relabel agent trajectories in the Craftax game with an LLM, DIAL [23] and SPRINT [28] relabel robot datasets for policy learning and pretraining, and CAST [7] and InstructVLA [25] augment VLA training with counterfactual instructions and multimodal instruction tuning. SOAR [32] is closest in applying a VLM to autonomously collected robot data, where it proposes tasks and detects success, but it improves the policy with goal-conditioned behavior cloning rather than RL. In these works, relabeling adds supervision to existing data to broaden the range of instructions a policy can follow. LfH uses relabeling for a different purpose. It targets a task the policy cannot yet solve, relabels the policy’s own failures on that task during online RL, and trains on the tasks those failures already accomplish so that progress transfers back to the target.

Learned Reward Models. Reward shaping provides learning signal when successes are rare by rewarding intermediate progress [16]. Recent work learns such rewards from visual data, as goal- or language-conditioned value functions [15, 14], from demonstrations [13, 11, 27], or from preference labels [22]. These models refine how a rollout is scored under its commanded instruction. LfH instead changes which instruction the rollout is credited for, which requires inferring what it accomplished and lets it provide signal even when it makes no progress on the commanded task.

3 Preliminaries

We study RL fine-tuning of VLA policies [3, 9]. At the start of each episode, the environment samples an instruction g∼Pgg\sim P_{g} that defines a target task and an initial RGB observation o0o_{0}. A policy πθ\pi_{\theta} rolls out actions at∼πθ(⋅∣ot,g)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid o_{t},g) for TT steps, yielding a trajectory τ=(o0,a0,…,aT−1,oT)\tau=(o_{0},a_{0},\ldots,a_{T-1},o_{T}) that receives a binary success reward R⁡(τ,g)R(\tau,g), equal to 11 when τ\tau completes gg and 00 otherwise. The objective is to maximize expected success J(θ)=𝔼g∼Pg,τ∼πθ(⋅∣g)[R(τ,g)]J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim P_{g},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid g)}[R(\tau,g)].

We instantiate LfH with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [21]. For each instruction gg, GRPO samples a group of KK trajectories {τi}i=1K\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} from πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, scores them with Ri=R⁡(τi,g)R_{i}=R(\tau_{i},g), and normalizes advantages within the group:

4 Method: Learning from Hindsight (LfH)

Problem. A GRPO group provides no learning signal when all its trajectories receive the same reward. A weak initial policy fails most rollouts, so many groups receive all-zero rewards. These groups have zero normalized advantage in Eq. (1), contribute no policy gradient, and fine-tuning makes little progress. LfH recovers learning signal from these otherwise discarded trajectories.

Approach. A trajectory that fails under one instruction may succeed under another. In Figure 1, a robot commanded to “put the green container in the bowl” instead places the tape in the bowl. This rollout fails for g=“put the green container in the bowl”g=\text{``put the green container in the bowl''} but succeeds for the hindsight instruction g′=“put the tape in the bowl”g^{\prime}=\text{``put the tape in the bowl''}. LfH relabels failed trajectories with instructions describing what the robot actually accomplished, converting zero-reward samples (τ,g)(\tau,g) into successful examples (τ,g′)(\tau,g^{\prime}). The hindsight instruction g′g^{\prime} need not be drawn from PgP_{g}. It shares objects and skills with the commanded task, which the policy can later compose to solve that task, and in the low-success regime it provides signal where the commanded instruction gives none. LfH lets the policy learn from what it already manages to do before it can reliably solve the commanded tasks. Two questions remain: (1) how to generate hindsight-labeled data (Section 4.1), and (2) how to incorporate it into GRPO (Section 4.2).

4.1 Training Signals from Hindsight

For each commanded instruction gg, GRPO samples a group {τi}i=1K\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} and scores it with Ri=R⁡(τi,g)R_{i}=R(\tau_{i},g). LfH activates only on low-reward groups, i.e., those with mean reward 1K​∑iRi<η\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i}R_{i}<\eta. High-reward groups already reinforce the commanded behavior, so relabeling them may introduce redundant or noisy auxiliary supervision. Given a low-reward group, LfH converts it into a hindsight-labeled group in two steps.

Instruction relabeling. We infer an alternative instruction under which a failed rollout still provides supervision. Since robot rollouts may lack privileged object states or task annotations, the VLM relabeler ℳψ\mathcal{M}_{\psi} sees only the rollout video, i.e., RGB frames from a fixed camera, together with the list of objects 𝒪\mathcal{O} in the scene. LfH samples an anchor from the failed trajectories, i⋆∼Unif⁡({i:Ri=0})i^{\star}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{i:R_{i}=0\}), since successful trajectories already carry a reliable label. Not every failure is useful, because some trajectories contain only accidental motion. To avoid noisy instructions, the VLM first classifies whether the anchor contains meaningful behavior, and anchors labeled uninteresting are discarded. For the remaining anchors, the VLM generates a hindsight instruction g′g^{\prime} describing what the anchor did in terms of the objects present in the scene:

g′∼ℳψinst(⋅∣τi⋆,𝒪).g^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{inst}}_{\psi}(\cdot\mid\tau_{i^{\star}},\mathcal{O}). (5)

Reward relabeling. LfH then evaluates every trajectory in the group under the shared hindsight instruction g′g^{\prime}:

R~i=ℳψrew​(τi,g′)∈{0,0.5,1},\tilde{R}_{i}=\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{rew}}_{\psi}(\tau_{i},g^{\prime})\in\{0,0.5,1\}, (6)

where 11 denotes completion of g′g^{\prime}, 00 failure, and 0.50.5 an ambiguous outcome, so an uncertain judgment is not treated as a confident success or failure. A shared instruction is essential because GRPO computes advantages relative to other trajectories in the group, and relabeling each with a different instruction would make their rewards incomparable. This yields the hindsight group 𝒢~={(τi,g′,R~i)}i=1K\tilde{\mathcal{G}}=\{(\tau_{i},g^{\prime},\tilde{R}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{K}.

4.2 GRPO with Hindsight Relabeling

LfH treats the hindsight group as an ordinary GRPO group. The only structural change is that its trajectories sampled under the commanded instruction gg are optimized under a hindsight instruction g′g^{\prime}. The exact hindsight policy gradient (HPG) [18] corrects this shift by multiplying the action-probability ratio π⁡(as∣os,g′)/π⁡(as∣os,g)\pi(a_{s}\mid o_{s},g^{\prime})/\pi(a_{s}\mid o_{s},g) over the current and all earlier steps s≤ts\leq t. For long VLA horizons, however, these products vanish or explode as small per-step differences compound. On our rollouts, the median cumulative ratio is 1.9×10−121.9\times 10^{-12}, and 16.6%16.6\% of cumulative ratios underflow to zero. We therefore use the local per-step ratio:

r~i,t​(θ)=πθ​(ai,t∣oi,t,g′)πθold​(ai,t∣oi,t,g).\tilde{r}_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t},g^{\prime})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,t}\mid o_{i,t},g)}. (7)

Unlike the GRPO ratio in Eq. (2), Eq. (7) need not equal one at the start of an update, because the numerator and denominator condition on different instructions. It ignores how the instruction change affects earlier steps, so it is biased, but its variance stays low. The bias is small when gg and g′g^{\prime} induce similar action distributions, and in practice the median local ratio is 0.940.94. We define the hindsight objective ℒH​-​GRPO\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H\text{-}GRPO}} as Eqs. (1)–(4) with advantages A~i\tilde{A}_{i} computed from R~i\tilde{R}_{i}, the ratio r~i,t\tilde{r}_{i,t} in place of ri,tr_{i,t}, and the KL term evaluated under g′g^{\prime}. To limit the effect of noisy or mismatched relabels, we clip ℒH​-​GRPO\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H\text{-}GRPO}} before weighting it:

ℒLfH​(θ)=ℒGRPO​(θ)+λ​min⁡(ℒH​-​GRPO​(θ),c).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LfH}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)+\lambda\,\min\!\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{H\text{-}GRPO}}(\theta),c\right). (8)

Here, λ\lambda weights the hindsight objective and cc is its clipping threshold. We set cc near the 85th percentile of early-training hindsight objectives, so the cap binds only on the largest hindsight terms, and choose λ\lambda so the weighted hindsight term roughly matches the GRPO objective. The original GRPO objective is unchanged. Section A.2 reports the bias–variance analysis and ratio statistics; Section A.3 gives HPG ablations.

5 Experiments

We organize our experiments around the following questions: (1) Does LfH improve the sample efficiency of GRPO fine-tuning under sparse rewards? (Sections 5.1 and 5.2). (2) How does LfH improve sample efficiency? (Section 5.3). (3) Is LfH effective on a physical robot? (Section 5.4). Further results and analyses appear in Section A.

Unless otherwise specified, all methods are initialized from the same RLinf-Pi05-LIBERO-SFT checkpoint [5], which was trained with few-shot demonstrations on the four LIBERO task suites [12] in simulation. We implement LfH and the baselines in RLinf [5, 26]. LfH uses Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking-FP8 for both instruction relabeling and reward relabeling (Section 4.1); prompts and further examples appear in Sections B.1 and C. Trajectories are represented as sequences of video frames from the global camera facing the robot.

5.1 Illustrative Example

We use the LIBERO-90 task “close the microwave” to illustrate how LfH improves sample efficiency and helps RL overcome a cold start from a weak initial policy.

LfH recovers useful training data from failed rollouts. The initial policy has zero success on the target task. As a result, standard GRPO assigns nearly all trajectory groups all-zero rewards and discards them, as shown in Figure 2(a). In contrast, LfH retains nearly 80% of groups after hindsight relabeling. The remaining groups are discarded when the failures cannot be assigned a meaningful hindsight instruction and reward.

LfH improves learning under sparse rewards. These recovered training examples allow GRPO to update even before the policy succeeds on the original task. As shown in Figure 2(b), GRPO+LfH steadily improves on “close the microwave,” while standard GRPO remains at zero success.

Why can instruction relabeling help? Although the policy initially fails at “close the microwave,” its rollouts still contain behaviors that can be relabeled with meaningful instructions, such as “Put the mug inside the microwave” and “Pull the microwave door open.” These examples train the policy on objects and actions shared with the target task, including the microwave, the door, and the concept open, which is the opposite of close. We hypothesize that this allows the policy to reuse concepts learned from other relabeled instruction-trajectory pairs when learning the target instruction.

5.2 Can LfH improve sample efficiency?

Setup. We evaluate whether LfH can accelerate RL fine-tuning when the initial VLA policy is weak. To this end, we construct out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks from the LIBERO-PRO benchmark using its task perturbation. These tasks preserve the original scenes, object instances, and environment dynamics, but change the task specification, such as the instructed object, target state, or desired action. For example, a policy may have seen the same kitchen scene during SFT, but must now manipulate a new object or reach a different goal state. This setting isolates the central challenge of sample-efficient RL: improving from mostly failed rollouts.

Implementation & Baselines. We train each method separately on each of the four LIBERO-PRO suites (Spatial, Goal, Object, and Long), each containing 10 tasks, with task perturbations. We report results averaged across suites. Each run consists of 40 training steps, collecting 64 environment rollouts per step (8 groups of 8) for Spatial, Goal, and Object, and 512 rollouts per step (64 groups of 8) for Long. We report means and standard errors over four random seeds. We compare LfH with standard GRPO and GRPO with RoboMETER dense progress rewards [11]. Standard GRPO uses the sparse environment success reward for the original instruction, while GRPO+RoboMETER uses a dense reward measuring progress toward the same instruction. The latter tests whether denser reward feedback alone can account for the sample-efficiency gains of LfH.

Metric. During training, we periodically freeze the policy and evaluate it with 480 rollouts per suite. We compute normalized gain separately for each task and then macro-average across tasks, giving each task equal weight. Let SR0\mathrm{SR}_{0} denote the success rate of the initial policy, and let SRt\mathrm{SR}_{t} denote the evaluation success rate after tt training steps. We define Gain⁡(t)=SRtSR0−1.\mathrm{Gain}(t)=\frac{\mathrm{SR}_{t}}{\mathrm{SR}_{0}}-1. This metric measures how quickly each method improves relative to the initial checkpoint as training proceeds. Every LIBERO-PRO task in this experiment has SR0>0\mathrm{SR}_{0}>0, so the gain is always defined. The real-world task starts at zero success, so there we report raw success rates.

Results. Figure 3(a) demonstrates that LfH substantially improves sample efficiency. LfH matches GRPO’s plateau performance after only 6 training steps, whereas GRPO requires approximately 30 steps, a 5×5\times reduction in environment interactions. LfH also outperforms GRPO with RoboMETER dense rewards, suggesting that denser feedback alone is insufficient when the policy rarely makes progress toward the commanded instruction. By step 40, LfH outperforms GRPO across all four suites.

Figure 3(b) helps explain this gain. Following the default in RLinf [26], groups whose mean reward falls below a lower threshold or above an upper threshold are filtered out before the update, since their near-uniform rewards yield vanishing advantages in Eq. (1). Under this filter, GRPO and GRPO+RoboMETER retain only 20–40% of rollout groups. LfH retains 70–80%, because relabeling turns many filtered all-failure groups into hindsight groups with informative rewards.

Can more updates per rollout match LfH? We increase the number of update epochs for both GRPO and proximal policy optimization (PPO) [20], meaning that each method takes more gradient steps on every rollout batch. The GRPO sweep directly tests whether extra optimization can explain LfH’s gain, while PPO provides the same test with another standard RL algorithm. Figure 7 shows that more updates do not consistently help either method and can hurt; even the best variants remain below LfH. Thus, LfH benefits from extracting new supervision from failed trajectories, not simply from reusing the same data more often.

Generality. Finally, we test whether this benefit transfers beyond a single VLA backbone. We keep the suites, task perturbation, rollouts per step, and seeds from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} experiments. GR00T [2] and OpenVLA-OFT [9] improve more slowly under GRPO, so we train each until its GRPO baseline plateaus, which takes 200 steps for GR00T and 60 steps for OpenVLA-OFT. Figure 3(c) shows consistent gains across both VLAs; per-suite curves appear in Section A.5.

5.3 Analysis: How does LfH improve sample efficiency?

Can LfH performance gains be attributed to instruction augmentation or reward relabeling alone? We isolate the two steps in LfH: hindsight instruction relabeling and reward relabeling (Section 4). We compare against two ablations. Rephrase-only replaces the hindsight instruction g′g^{\prime} with a paraphrase of the original instruction gg while keeping the original rewards, testing whether language augmentation alone explains the gain. Reward-only keeps the instruction as gg but relabels rewards with the VLM, testing whether reward relabeling alone explains the gain. Both ablations improve only marginally over GRPO and stay well below LfH throughout training (Figure 4), so the benefit comes from coupling the two steps.

Can LfH performance gains be attributed to perturbed rewards? We next test whether LfH works simply because it injects reward variance into otherwise discarded groups. The random-reward baseline creates nonzero advantages without semantically meaningful hindsight labels, yet gains little (Figure 4). The benefit of LfH therefore comes from grounded hindsight labels, not from avoiding zero-variance groups.

When does LfH help the most? LfH is most effective when failures are diverse and semantically interpretable. Figure 9 shows sample rollouts at training step 40 on the microwave task. Standard GRPO produces many similar trajectories: the robot repeatedly approaches the same mug with similar gripper poses, leading to a low-diversity failure mode. In contrast, LfH rollouts show more varied object interactions and spatial configurations around the objects. Because these samples come after training has progressed, LfH may also help maintain behavioral diversity during RL fine-tuning, not only exploit diversity the initial policy already had. One possible explanation is that hindsight relabeling gives credit to multiple meaningful alternative behaviors, whereas GRPO treats them all as failures under the commanded task. As a result, GRPO can collapse toward repeated unsuccessful behaviors, while LfH continues to reinforce a broader set of grounded object interactions.

How does data diversity affect LfH? We vary π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s rollout noise to control trajectory diversity. Figure 8 shows an optimum for both methods: too little noise limits exploration, while too much produces incoherent rollouts. LfH benefits more near this optimum because it can relabel diverse failures as meaningful alternative tasks, whereas GRPO benefits only when exploration improves reward on the commanded task.

5.4 Real-world results

Setup. We evaluate LfH on a real Franka FR3 robot with manipulable objects, two drawers, and a two-level rack. We first perform SFT on π0.5\pi_{0.5} with 9 language-conditioned manipulation tasks using 20 SpaceMouse demonstrations per task, spanning short pick-and-place and longer multi-stage tasks. We then fine-tune on a held-out task, put the green container in the bowl, where the initial SFT policy has zero success. Both GRPO and GRPO+LfH use the same binary human reward. See Section B.2 for details and Section B for implementation settings.

Results. Figure 5 shows that LfH improves real-world sample efficiency. Both methods start from zero, but LfH improves faster. At 128 rollouts, LfH achieves roughly twice the success rate of GRPO; at 160 rollouts, LfH reaches 56%56\% success, while GRPO plateaus at 22%22\%.

Analysis. The initial policy often grounds instructions to the wrong object, for example grasping the tape regardless of the commanded instruction. GRPO treats these rollouts only as failures. LfH instead relabels them with instructions describing the executed behavior, such as “pick up the tape” or “move the tape to the bowl,” turning failed target-task attempts into useful supervision for object grounding and manipulation.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

More bits per robot sample. LfH is motivated by a simple question: how many useful bits do we extract from each costly robot rollout? Classic RL uses a rollout mainly to evaluate whether the intended outcome happened, often reducing a rich trajectory to one reward. This is inefficient when physical interaction is expensive. Following the broader view that learning systems should extract more information from each sample [10], LfH treats a trajectory as evidence for multiple language goals consistent with what happened. In this sense, hindsight relabeling increases the bits per sample: one rollout can supervise multiple possible tasks, rather than only the task originally commanded.

Practical implication. This is especially natural for pretrained VLAs. Because these models already generalize across related language instructions, training on what the robot actually did can improve what it was asked to do. LfH therefore changes the role of robot data: failed attempts are no longer merely negative examples, but reusable experience that can be mined for nearby tasks. This offers a practical path for VLA post-training: instead of only collecting more rollouts or taking more optimization steps on the same labels, we can reinterpret each rollout through language and transfer learning across the tasks it supports.

Limitations. LfH is limited by the behaviors present in the collected data. If the policy produces repetitive or uninformative trajectories, there are few meaningful hindsight goals to recover. It also depends on relabeling quality, since incorrect or overly generic instructions introduce noisy supervision. Better filtering, uncertainty estimation, and lightweight human verification are important directions for reliable deployment.

Appendix A Extended Experimental Results

A.1 Additional ablation studies

Figure 6 collects the group-selection, prompt, and VLM-size ablations discussed below.

Relabeled group selection. We relabel only groups whose mean original-task reward falls below the threshold η=0.8\eta=0.8, unless otherwise specified. This targets groups with enough failures to yield useful hindsight supervision while avoiding the compute and noisy or redundant updates caused by relabeling successful groups.

Figure 6(a) compares our 0.8 threshold with two variants: random selection of the same 70% of groups and relabeling all groups. Thresholding performs substantially better than both. Random selection wastes VLM queries on uninformative groups, while relabeling all groups can dilute useful original-task supervision with redundant or noisy hindsight updates.

We also ablate the threshold used for filtering groups. As shown in Figure 6(b), a very low threshold, such as 0.1, relabels only all-failed groups and therefore misses many trajectories that fail the commanded task but still contain meaningful, reusable object interactions. A more moderate threshold, such as 0.5, improves over this stricter setting but still underperforms the default threshold of 0.8. LfH thus benefits most from relabeling a broad set of non-saturated groups.

VLM prompt. LfH uses two structured templates. For instruction relabeling, the VLM receives a rollout and a list of scene objects, then returns a concise instruction describing the achieved behavior or Nothing if no meaningful interaction occurred. For reward relabeling, it receives the rollout and proposed hindsight instruction, then classifies completion as success, failure, or unsure, mapped to rewards 1, 0, and 0.5, respectively. On LIBERO-PRO Goal with task perturbation using π0.5\pi_{0.5}, we ablate the object list and the two abstention options. Figure 6(c) shows that removing any component reduces sample efficiency. Without the object list, labels become less grounded and consistent; without Nothing, idle or contact-free rollouts become noisy positive examples; without unsure, ambiguous videos receive potentially incorrect binary rewards. Thus, effective relabeling requires prompts that constrain labels and permit filtering or abstention.

Weaker VLM. We also evaluate LfH with Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking: it retains most of the 235B VLM’s gain and clearly outperforms GRPO (Figure 6(d)).

Figure 7 compares update epochs for GRPO (panel 7(a)) and PPO (panel 7(b)).

A.2 Additional analysis of LfH

Figure 9 contrasts the microwave rollouts under GRPO (panel 9(a)) and LfH (panel 9(b)).

Hindsight correction diagnostics. Equation (7) trades the unbiasedness of full HPG for much lower variance over long VLA horizons. Empirically, the median local ratio is 0.940.94, whereas the median cumulative HPG ratio is 1.9×10−121.9\times 10^{-12}; 16.6%16.6\% of cumulative ratios underflow to zero, and the largest 10%10\% carry 68.7%68.7\% of the total weight. Both literal HPG and a self-normalized variant underperform standard GRPO.

Can LfH improve sample efficiency on other OOD perturbations? We next evaluate a less obvious setting for language-based hindsight: position perturbations. Here, the commanded language prompt is unchanged, but the initial object positions are shifted. Since LfH relabels trajectories in language space, it is not immediately clear that it should help when only the environment configuration changes. Surprisingly, the preliminary results in Figure 15 suggest that LfH can still improve over GRPO on position-perturbation tasks, both in sample efficiency and maximum success rate. This points to a possible broader benefit of LfH: relabeled failures may help the policy reuse experience from shifted layouts and learn object interactions that can transfer back to the commanded task.

A.3 Additional mechanism and robustness analyses

Instruction–behavior pairing. In a follow-up analysis of the converged microwave policy, mug-directed behavior under “close the microwave” dropped to 0%0\% as task success rose from 0%0\% to 94%94\%. We also permuted hindsight instructions across rollout groups while keeping the trajectories, rewards, and advantages fixed. Microwave success fell from 94%94\% to 0%0\%, indicating that the instruction–behavior pairing matters beyond introducing reward variation.

Hindsight correction and VLM size. The single-step cross-instruction ratio avoids the weight degeneration of cumulative per-decision HPG [18]: 16.6%16.6\% of cumulative ratios underflow to zero, and the largest 10%10\% carry 68.7%68.7\% of total weight. Unclipped HPG and a self-normalized variant both underperform GRPO, while LfH remains stable. The smaller Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking relabeler retains most of the 235B model’s gain and outperforms GRPO. Figure 10 shows these comparisons: panel 10(a) compares HPG estimators, and panel 10(b) compares VLM sizes.

Language-relabeling baseline. We adapted Hindsight Instruction Relabeling (HIR) [29] to the online LIBERO-PRO Goal setting, imitating each relabeled trajectory with a contrastive loss. By step 20, HIR reached ±0.6%1.5\!\pm\!0.6\%, compared with ±2.6%22.8\!\pm\!2.6\% for GRPO and ±1.3%29.1\!\pm\!1.3\% for LfH.

Cross-suite transfer. Policies trained on LIBERO-PRO Object were evaluated on LIBERO-PRO Spatial instructions with unseen tasks and scenes. LfH performed better on five of eight instructions, tied on two, and performed worse on one.

Appendix B Implementation details

B.1 LfH experimental details

Hyperparameters.

For the 64-rollout simulation experiments, we use 6464 environments with one rollout collection per step. We use group size K=8K=8, microbatch 3232, global batch 512512, KL​_​beta=0\mathrm{KL\_beta}=0 (no KL penalty), two gradient update epochs, and VLM relabeling temperature 0.80.8.

Prompts.

LfH uses the VLM to both relabel the prompt and also assign rewards. The relabeling prompt is:

The reward prompt is:

LfH group selection.

Trajectories are grouped into sets of K=8K{=}8. Groups whose mean reward falls within [θlow,θhigh]=[0.8,1.0][\theta_{\text{low}},\theta_{\text{high}}]=[0.8,1.0] are skipped; all other groups (mean reward <0.8<0.8) are selected for hindsight relabeling. This focuses relabeling on groups with substantial failure rates where hindsight instructions provide the most value, while leaving near-saturated groups untouched.

Hindsight loss clipping.

LfH can occasionally produce very large hindsight-policy losses, especially early in training when hindsight rewards are noisy. To prevent a small number of hindsight groups from dominating optimization, we clip the hindsight GRPO loss before applying the hindsight weight:

LLfH​(θ)=LGRPO​(θ)+λ⋅min⁡(LH​-​GRPO​(θ),c),L_{\mathrm{LfH}}(\theta)=L_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)+\lambda\cdot\min\left(L_{\mathrm{H\text{-}GRPO}}(\theta),c\right),

where cc is a clipping threshold and λ\lambda controls the overall contribution of hindsight updates. This bounds the maximum contribution of the hindsight term to λ​c\lambda c, while leaving the standard GRPO objective unchanged.

We keep this maximum hindsight contribution fixed across all experiments. To set the clipping threshold, we estimate the empirical distribution of hindsight losses during the early stage of training and choose cc as approximately the 85th percentile. We then choose λ\lambda such that the weighted LfH batch loss is roughly equal to the original batch policy loss.

Same-instruction skip.

Before reward evaluation, any trajectory whose relabeled instruction matches the original task (after case/punctuation normalization) reverts to its original instruction and environment reward, avoiding redundant VLM queries.

Policy likelihoods.

For flow-matching policies (π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T), we follow the flow-to-SDE reformulation, modeling the NN-step denoising trajectory as Gaussian transitions 𝒩⁡(μθ​(xi,ti,o,g),σi2​I)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(x_{i},t_{i},o,g),\sigma_{i}^{2}I), with μθ\mu_{\theta} obtained from the predicted velocity, and sum their log densities. For OpenVLA-OFT, we sum the per-token categorical log probabilities of its discrete action tokens. In both cases the cross-instruction ratio rescores the same executed trajectory under g′g^{\prime}, changing only the instruction conditioning.

VLM computation.

VLM relabeling and reward evaluation took approximately 155155 seconds per training step on a separate node with eight H100 GPUs.

B.2 Real-world experimental details

Setup. Our real-world setup consists of a Franka FR3 arm, a set of manipulable objects, two drawers, and a two-level rack. We first fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} with supervised learning (SFT) on 9 language-conditioned tasks that span different difficulty levels and horizon lengths, from short-horizon pick-and-place to multi-stage manipulation. For each task, we collect 2020 demonstration rollouts using SpaceMouse teleoperation. Figure 16 shows the real-world setup. Table 1 lists the SFT task prompts.

RL fine-tuning. We then compare GRPO and GRPO+LfH on the task put the green container in the bowl, where the initial SFT policy achieves zero success. Rewards are provided by a human operator as binary labels. Each rollout has a time limit of 3030 seconds, corresponding to 512512 action steps; each step executes an action chunk of size 1616 predicted by the VLA model. For each of GRPO and GRPO+LfH, we use 32 rollouts per training step (160 total) and evaluate on separate rollouts after each training step. Each real-world method was evaluated with one training seed. Tables 2 and 3 list the GRPO and SFT hyperparameters, respectively.
